Chronicle of an 800-Year Landmark

History of Grace Dieu Priory

Founded in 1239 by a remarkable feudal noblewoman and rescued from dereliction by volunteers in 1995. Explore eight centuries of monastic devotion, literary heritage, and community conservation.

Founder Profile

The Remarkable Life of Roesia de Verdun

In an era when medieval women rarely held autonomous feudal power, Roesia (Rose) de Verdun was an extraordinary exception. The de Verdun dynasty were influential Anglo-Norman nobles with extensive territories across England, Ireland, and the Welsh Marches.

When no male heir survived to inherit the family lands, Roesia stepped forward to take direct control of the estates. She paid a substantial fine of 700 marks to King Henry III for the right to remain an unmarried widow and rule her properties in her own name. So formidable was her leadership that King Henry III commended her for defending and securing her borders in Ireland—a feat none of her male forebears had achieved.

Between 1235 and 1241, Roesia established Grace Dieu Priory in the secluded Charnwood valley, dedicating it to the Augustinian canonesses. Upon her death in 1247, she was interred in the priory church. Following the 1538 Dissolution, local villagers re-interred her magnificent stone tomb inside St John the Baptist Church in Belton, where her sculpted effigy can still be admired today.

Tomb Location: St John the Baptist Church, Belton (2 miles from Priory)

Chronicle

Eight Centuries of History: 1235 to the Present

Step through the pivotal milestones that shaped Grace Dieu from an independent nunnery to a public sanctuary.

1235–1241Monastic Foundation

Foundation of Gratia Dei (Grace of God)

Founded by the Norman-Irish noblewoman Roesia (Rose) de Verdun as an independent priory for Augustinian canonesses (nuns dedicated to St Mary and the Holy Trinity). The foundation charter was formally confirmed by the famous scholar-bishop Robert Grosseteste of Lincoln, granting the house freedom from diocesan taxation and monastic subordination.

✦ Named "Gratia Dei" (Grace of God) in recognition of divine favor.
1377Community Care

Monastic Expansion & The Almonry Hospital

By 1377, the priory had blossomed into a flourishing religious community of 16 canonesses. In addition to their daily monastic liturgy and agricultural estate duties, the nuns operated an almonry hospital within the precinct, providing daily food, hospice care, and shelter to 12 poor individuals from the surrounding Charnwood parishes.

✦ Demonstrating the priory’s pivotal role as a medical and social lifeline.
1414–1418Estate Chronicles

Dame Petronella’s Monastic Account Book

During the prioress-ship of Dame Petronella, clerks maintained a rare working draft account book. Unlike formal manorial accounts which were routinely discarded, this 348-page manuscript survived. It meticulously details tenant rents across Leicestershire, purchases of salted herrings, salmon, and beef, building maintenance wages, servant stipends, and expenses for celebrating holy feast days.

✦ An internationally celebrated window into early 15th-century everyday monastic life.
View the Published Account Book in our Shop ›
1538Tudor Era

The Dissolution & The Beaumont Manor

In October 1538, King Henry VIII’s commissioners dissolved Grace Dieu Priory. The site was purchased by John Beaumont, Master of the Rolls, who remodeled the cloister buildings into a magnificent Tudor mansion. The estate became the family seat and birthplace of his grandsons: Sir John Beaumont (the metaphysical poet) and Francis Beaumont (the renowned Jacobean dramatist who collaborated with John Fletcher).

✦ Transitioning from sacred cloister to literary Renaissance cradle.
1995–2006Volunteer Salvation

The Rescue: Ivy Removal to Public Reopening

By the late 20th century, the abandoned mansion had collapsed into dangerous ruins enveloped in dense ivy and scrub. In 1995, local residents formed the Grace Dieu Priory Charitable Trust to prevent total loss. Over a ten-year conservation project (1996–2006), specialist stonemasons cleared tonnes of vegetation and stabilized surviving cloister arches, before officially reopening the site free of charge to the public in 2006.

✦ Over a decade of voluntary labor saved this ancient monument for the nation.
2024Modern Milestone

Permanent Freehold Site Ownership Secured

In November 2024, following two years of sensitive negotiations with private landowners, The Grace Dieu Priory Trust officially acquired the freehold of the entire monument and Rusty Mary’s field. No longer tenants, the Trust now possesses the permanent authority to initiate scheduled archaeological excavations and construct a new accessible footbridge for future generations.

✦ Securing the monument’s future under charity ownership.

Visitor Code

Leave No TracePlease take all of your litter home with you. There are no public waste bins on the ancient monument ruins.
Dog WalkersDogs welcome on leads. A dedicated bin is located at the Bull's Head car park for dog litter bags (strictly none on-site).
Strict Site Policy: Paranormal events and ghost walks are expressly forbidden by the Grace Dieu Priory Trust across the entire priory site and surrounding lands.
